title: How Should We Write a Curriculum?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles responds to a headteacher's claim that curriculum choices are driven by happenstance rather than design by checking that school's outcomes against similar-intake schools. His larger argument is about school leadership: strong values and conviction keep leaders in post, but those same values can lead them to be less effective for students. He names prominent blogging heads whose schools had disappointing Progress 8 results to make the point. His remedy is to stay passionate while testing every opinion against measured student progress. He frames this as both arrogance (certainty based on impact) and humility (willingness to be shown wrong). The piece ends with a book plug, and its use of named individuals is blunt.
points: Values are a survival mechanism for school leaders, but they can quietly make leaders less effective if never tested.
Salles benchmarks a school against similar-intake schools, using FFT Compare Schools rankings rather than raw Progress 8 alone.
The prescribed discipline is to hold strong values while testing every opinion against student progress in your classroom, department or school.
Treating opinions as bets that evidence can overturn is presented as both a humility practice and a source of confidence.
quotes: A head needs strong values, and the resilience to stick to them in the face of an ever growing and mutating list of challenges.
Having strong values is probably the Darwinian survival mechanism that keeps us in post. But what if it also makes us less effective?
Be passionate. Insist on strong values. But test every single opinion you have against the progress of the students in your classroom, department or school.

Any belief may turn out to be wrong. This has been so valuable for me that I now spend much of my time looking for proof that I may be wrong. It also gives me much more confidence in the opinions that remain … until the evidence says otherwise.
In fact, once behaviour is good in the classroom, nothing I know will transform the progress of your students quicker than an intentionally designed curriculum.
